newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: New Lithuania finance minister cautious on plans.
newsitem.headline: New Lithuania finance minister cautious on plans.

text.p: Lithuania's new finance minister Rolandas Matiuliauskas was cautious on Friday over the policies he would pursue but made clear he was keen on foreign investment.
The 28-year-old businessman said he would take time to form a judgement on the new government's key policy of unpegging the litas currency from the dollar and ending the currency board system.
"Probably later, when I get to know all the details, then I will be able to tell if radical reforms are necessary," he told journalists.
Asked for his views on privatisation, he replied that he was keen on the idea.
"If a company or people, say honest people from Lithuania and abroad, are interested in investing, then why not?" he said. "We would have more money for other needs."

The new coalition government of two right-of-centre parties, led by Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius, ousted the former Communists, who were praised for stabilising the economy and cutting inflation but criticised for their reluctance to privatise key state industries.

One of the new government's most controversial policies is to end the litas's four-to-one peg to the dollar, which is administered under a currency board. This obliges the central bank to keep enough reserves to back the local currency in circulation but it is stripped of all its other powers to influence monetary policy.
Matiuliauskas said, "For private business it is okay when I as a businessman do not have to worry about a rising exchange rate but from a macroeconomic point of view, few countries use this method."
The new finance minister is currently head of a Lithuanian-German joint enterprise, Interpharma, which is in the wholesale medicine business.

He graduated from Vilnius University and helped draw up regulations for introducing international accountancy standards in Lithuania. He has also worked in the finance ministry and spent two months with Barclays Bank in Toronto. -- Riga Newsroom, +371 721 5240
